title: HTML Text and Headings
subtitle: Organise content into clear, meaningful sections
description: Learn how to structure headings, paragraphs, emphasis, quotations, and text-level content so webpages are readable, accessible, and logically organised.

blocks.text: Welcome! Let's organise webpage content

Welcome back! In Lesson 1, you learned that HTML describes the structure and meaning of webpage content. Now let's apply that knowledge to something you see on almost every website: written text. Imagine opening a learning website where the title, instructions, examples, and explanations all appear as one long block of words. Even if every word is correct, the page would be difficult to understand. Good HTML structure helps readers recognise topics, follow ideas, and find information quickly.

In this lesson, you will learn more than how to make text look large or bold. You will learn how to express the role of each piece of content. A main heading identifies the page's primary topic. Subheadings organise smaller topics. Paragraphs contain connected sentences. Strong emphasis marks important content, while emphasis can indicate stress or a change in meaning. By the end, you should be able to create a page with a clear reading hierarchy rather than a collection of unrelated text.
Section 1 — Understanding heading levels

HTML provides six heading elements: h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, and h6. They represent six levels of headings, from the highest level to the lowest. Think of a textbook: the book title identifies the main subject, chapter titles identify major sections, and smaller headings divide chapters into topics. HTML headings can express a similar hierarchy. For example, h1 can identify the main topic of a page, h2 can identify a major section, and h3 can identify a subsection within that section.

A common beginner mistake is choosing a heading element only because its default text size looks attractive. Suppose h2 looks the right size for a small label. It may be tempting to use it even when the content is actually a minor subsection of an h2 section. Instead, choose the heading level according to the content's place in the document hierarchy. You can later use CSS to make any heading larger, smaller, heavier, or more colourful without changing its meaning.

Heading levels should communicate a logical structure. A page might begin with an h1 called Web Development, followed by an h2 called HTML Fundamentals. Within that section, an h3 called Headings and Paragraphs could introduce a more specific topic. After that subsection ends, another h2 could introduce CSS Fundamentals. You do not have to use every heading level on every page. Use the levels that accurately represent the content, and avoid jumping between levels without a reason.

blocks.title: Sample 1 — Create a logical heading hierarchy
blocks.code:
Web Development

HTML Fundamentals

Headings and Paragraphs

HTML gives content a meaningful structure.

Links and Images

Links connect resources, and images add visual information.

CSS Fundamentals

CSS controls the presentation of webpage content.
blocks.output: A page with one main heading, two major sections, and related subsections under HTML Fundamentals.

blocks.text: Study the relationship in the example. Headings and Paragraphs and Links and Images are both h3 elements because they are subsections of HTML Fundamentals. CSS Fundamentals is another h2 because it introduces a new major section at the same level as HTML Fundamentals. The goal is not to create a perfect-looking outline by guessing font sizes. The goal is to make the organisation understandable to people and software that interpret the page structure.

blocks.question: You are documenting a course. The main topic is HTML, its major section is Forms, and a subsection within Forms is Validation. Which heading sequence most clearly represents that hierarchy?
options:
HTML

Forms

Validation

HTML

Forms

Validation

HTML

Forms

Validation

HTML

Forms

Validation
blocks.explanation: The h1 identifies the main topic, h2 introduces a major section, and h3 identifies a subsection within that section. This sequence communicates the intended hierarchy clearly.
blocks.hint: Match the heading level to the relationship between the main topic, section, and subsection.

blocks.text: Section 2 — Writing paragraphs and readable content

The p element represents a paragraph. Use it for a connected group of sentences that forms a unit of prose, such as an introduction, an explanation, or a short description. Browsers normally display paragraphs as separate blocks with spacing around them. This default spacing makes one paragraph easier to distinguish from another, but the exact appearance can change with CSS and browser settings.

Do not use a paragraph merely because you want some vertical space. Paragraphs communicate the structure of prose. If you want more space between sections, CSS is the appropriate tool. If you want to represent a list of steps, use list elements rather than writing every step as an unrelated paragraph. Choosing the correct structure makes your document easier to maintain when the design changes.

HTML usually collapses runs of ordinary spaces and line breaks in the source into a single displayed space. For example, placing five spaces between two words in your source does not normally produce five spaces on the page. Likewise, pressing Enter in your editor does not automatically create a new visible paragraph. Use paragraph elements to separate paragraphs, and use the appropriate elements for lists, headings, and other content. CSS controls visual spacing and line layout.

Readable content depends on more than correct tags. Give each paragraph one main idea, explain unfamiliar terms, and place related ideas together. A very long paragraph can be difficult to scan, especially on a phone. Several tiny paragraphs can also interrupt the flow unnecessarily. Think about the learner or reader: what should they understand first, and what information do they need next? Good structure helps your reader follow that journey.

blocks.title: Sample 2 — Separate ideas into paragraphs
blocks.code:
Why I Am Learning HTML

HTML helps me describe the structure and meaning of webpage content.

I can use headings to organise topics and paragraphs to explain each idea.

After learning the structure, I can use CSS to improve the design and JavaScript to add interaction.
blocks.output: A heading followed by three distinct paragraphs, each expressing a related but separate idea.

blocks.text: Try editing the sample. Combine the second and third paragraphs into one paragraph, then preview the page. The words may remain almost identical, but the content structure changes. Next, separate them again and give each paragraph one main idea. This exercise helps you understand that HTML is not simply a way to display words; it lets you organise those words into meaningful parts.

blocks.question: A learner presses Enter several times in an HTML file to separate two sentences, but the browser displays them close together. Which solution most accurately represents two separate paragraphs?
options: Wrap each sentence in its own p element.
Insert multiple ordinary spaces between the sentences and leave them in one text block.
Add several h1 elements between the sentences to force paragraph spacing.
Put the second sentence in the document title so the browser separates it automatically.
blocks.explanation: Separate p elements explicitly identify separate paragraphs. Ordinary whitespace in HTML source is usually collapsed, so pressing Enter or adding spaces alone does not reliably create paragraph structure.
blocks.hint: Use the element whose purpose is to represent a paragraph.

blocks.text: Section 3 — Strong importance, emphasis, and inline text

Sometimes you need to identify an important warning or emphasise a word inside a sentence. HTML provides elements for these purposes. The strong element represents strong importance, seriousness, or urgency. The em element represents stress emphasis that can affect the meaning of a sentence. Browsers commonly display both in distinctive styles, often bold for strong and italic for em, but their meaning matters more than their default appearance.

Consider the sentence, 'You must save your work before closing the editor.' You could mark 'must' with em if the stress is important to the sentence, or use strong for a serious instruction or warning. The choice depends on the meaning you intend. Do not select strong merely because you want bold letters, or em merely because you want italic letters. CSS can change appearance while the HTML continues to communicate the correct meaning.

You may also encounter b and i. These elements draw attention to text without necessarily expressing the same importance or stress as strong and em. For example, a keyword in an article may be visually distinguished with b, while a technical term or title may be marked with i depending on its context. The correct choice depends on the content and the conventions of the document. For meaningful emphasis, strong and em are often the better starting points.

Another useful element is mark, which represents text highlighted for reference or relevance in the current context. The small element is used for side comments or fine print. The del element represents content that has been deleted from a document, while ins represents inserted content. These elements are not interchangeable decorations: each communicates a particular meaning. You will not need every one in every project, but understanding their purpose helps you select suitable markup when the situation arises.

blocks.title: Sample 3 — Mark text according to its meaning
blocks.code:
Important Study Advice

Save your work before closing the editor.

You should always check your code before publishing.

Today's topic is HTML text structure.

Old deadline: Monday New deadline: Wednesday.
blocks.output: A heading followed by important advice, stressed wording, highlighted text, and an updated deadline.

blocks.text: Notice that strong, em, mark, del, and ins can appear inside a paragraph. They are inline elements: they form part of the surrounding text rather than automatically creating a separate paragraph. They can also be nested when the combination is meaningful and valid. As always, close nested elements in the correct order. Avoid adding elements only to force a visual effect when their meaning does not match your content.

blocks.question: An online examination page warns that a submission cannot be changed after it is sent. You want the warning to communicate serious importance, not merely a visual style. Which markup is the strongest semantic choice?
options: You cannot change your submission.
You cannot change your submission.
<mark>You cannot change your submission.</mark> in every context, because mark always means a serious warning.
You cannot change your submission., because b and strong have exactly the same semantic meaning.
blocks.explanation: Strong communicates strong importance or seriousness. The b element draws attention without necessarily conveying that importance, i does not express the same meaning, and mark highlights text relevant to the current context.
blocks.hint: Choose the element whose meaning expresses strong importance.

blocks.text: Section 4 — Quotations, line breaks, and special text

HTML includes elements for presenting quotations. The blockquote element represents a quotation from another source that is presented as a separate block. The q element represents a short inline quotation. Browsers may add quotation marks around q content automatically, depending on their default styles and language settings. When a quotation has a source, you can use the cite attribute on blockquote to identify the source URL, although the attribute does not automatically create a visible citation label.

The br element creates a line break within content where a line break is part of the intended meaning, such as an address or a poem. It should not be used repeatedly to create large empty spaces between unrelated sections. Use separate paragraphs for separate paragraphs and CSS for layout spacing. The hr element represents a thematic break between sections, often displayed as a horizontal line. It is not simply a decorative line to insert wherever a page needs more visual detail.

HTML also has character references for characters that have special meaning in markup. For example, a less-than sign can be written as < and an ampersand as &. This matters when you want to show code such as

to a reader rather than have the browser interpret it as an element. The browser interprets valid markup as structure, so characters that would otherwise begin markup or a character reference need to be written appropriately when they are intended to appear as text.

For example, to display the literal text

Hello

as a teaching example, write <h1>Hello</h1> in the HTML source. The browser then displays the angle brackets and words rather than creating a heading from that text. This technique is especially useful when building tutorials, documentation, and code examples. In a real HTML code editor, you usually write the actual tags; in an article explaining those tags, you may need character references to display them literally.

blocks.title: Sample 4 — Quotations and displaying markup as text
blocks.code:
Notes from My Teacher

Practise regularly and learn from your mistakes.

My teacher said, Understand the reason behind your code.

To create a heading, write <h1>Title</h1>.

End of lesson notes.
blocks.output: A page showing a block quotation, an inline quotation, and literal HTML markup inside a code element.

blocks.text: In the final paragraph of the sample, code is used to identify a short fragment of computer code. The character references make the tag appear literally instead of being interpreted as a heading. This is an important difference between writing HTML that creates content and writing HTML that teaches someone about HTML. When you build educational pages, examples often need to show tags exactly as written, so understanding character references will help you avoid confusing output.

blocks.question: You are creating an HTML tutorial. The page must visibly show the literal tag <h2> without creating an actual heading from it. Which source fragment achieves that?
options: <h2>

Heading tag

, because the literal opening tag will always be printed as text.

&h2;

, because every tag name can be displayed by adding an ampersand before it.
blocks.explanation: The character references < and > display the less-than and greater-than characters as text. The code element identifies the fragment as code, while the browser does not interpret the escaped characters as a real heading tag.
blocks.hint: You need to display the angle brackets as characters instead of using them to begin markup.

blocks.text: Section 5 — Build a well-structured article

Now bring everything together. Imagine you are building an article for a student learning platform. The article needs one main heading, a short introduction, a major section about practice, a subsection about reviewing mistakes, a quotation from a teacher, and an important reminder. Before writing the code, decide the relationship between these pieces. Which heading introduces the article? Which heading introduces a major section? Which heading belongs under that section? Planning the structure first will help you avoid random tag choices.

Start with h1 for the article's main topic. Use p elements for the introduction and explanations. Use h2 for the major section and h3 for a subsection within it. If a statement needs to communicate strong importance, consider strong. If a phrase needs stress emphasis, consider em. Use blockquote for a separate quotation and q for a short quotation within a sentence. Each element has a specific job, and the combination should make the content easier to understand.

After writing the page, inspect its structure instead of judging only its appearance. Ask whether the headings make sense when read as an outline. Check whether each paragraph contains a coherent idea. Confirm that emphasis matches the intended meaning. Verify that opening and closing tags are paired correctly and nested in the correct order. If the page looks plain, do not assume the HTML is wrong: styling belongs primarily to CSS, which you will learn in your CSS course.

Here is a practical challenge: create an article titled Learning Through Practice. Add an introductory paragraph, an h2 section called Build Small Projects, and an h3 subsection called Review Your Mistakes. Include a sentence with strong emphasis and a quotation from a teacher. Preview the result, then change the heading hierarchy and observe how the document's organisation changes. Try to write the structure yourself before checking earlier examples. This is how you turn knowledge into a skill.

blocks.question: A tutorial article has a main heading, a section called Debugging, and a smaller topic called Finding a Missing File within Debugging. It also includes a separate quotation from a teacher. Which implementation best matches both the heading hierarchy and quotation structure?
options:
Article

Debugging

Finding a Missing File

Teacher quotation

Article

Debugging

Finding a Missing File

Check the file path carefully.

Article

Debugging

Finding a Missing File

Check the file path carefully.

Debugging

Finding a Missing File

Check the file path carefully.
blocks.explanation: The h1 identifies the article, h2 introduces the major Debugging section, and h3 identifies a subsection. The blockquote correctly represents a separate quotation. The other choices fail to communicate the intended hierarchy or use elements for the wrong purpose.
blocks.hint: Look for the correct sequence of heading levels and the element designed for a separate quotation.

blocks.text: Lesson recap — You can now organise written content

Well done! You have learned how heading levels communicate hierarchy, how paragraphs separate connected ideas, and how strong and em communicate meaning beyond their usual visual styles. You have also explored quotations, line breaks, thematic breaks, inline code, and character references. These elements give your webpage a more deliberate structure and help readers understand how each piece of content fits into the whole.

Before moving forward, build the practice article without copying the examples line by line. If you can choose suitable headings, separate paragraphs, add emphasis with a clear reason, and display a short HTML tag literally, you have understood the central skills of this lesson. In Lesson 3, you will learn how to create links and connect pages together. Remember: good web development begins with understanding why each element belongs in the document, not simply memorising tag names.
